description.en: Learn Python threading and multiprocessing basics — when to use each, the GIL, and how to parallelize work safely.

story_variants.en:
## The Parallel Kitchen

A restaurant kitchen has **multiple chefs** working simultaneously. Some share one stove (threads share memory); others have their own kitchen entirely (processes have separate memory).

### Threading vs Multiprocessing vs Async

| Approach | Best For | Memory | GIL affected? |
|----------|----------|--------|---------------|
| `threading` | I/O-bound | shared | Yes |
| `multiprocessing` | CPU-bound | separate | No |
| `asyncio` | I/O-bound | shared | Yes |

### The GIL
> The **Global Interpreter Lock** (GIL) allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads can still be useful for I/O — while one thread waits for network, another runs.

### Key Classes
- `threading.Thread(target=func)` — create a thread
- `thread.start()` — launch it
- `thread.join()` — wait for it to finish
- `multiprocessing.Process` — same API, separate process
- `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` — high-level pool

> **Rule of thumb:** Use `threading` for I/O-bound (web scraping, file ops). Use `multiprocessing` for CPU-bound (number crunching, image processing).
story_variants.ta:
## பாரலல் சமையலறை

ஒரு உணவகச் சமையலறையில் **பல சமையல்காரர்கள்** ஒரே நேரத்தில் வேலை செய்கிறார்கள். சிலர் ஒரே தீப்பொறி (threads share memory) பகிர்ந்து கொள்கிறார்கள்; மற்றவர்களுக்கு தனித்த சமையலறை இருக்கிறது (processes have separate memory).

### Threading vs Multiprocessing vs Async

| அணுகுமுறை | சிறந்தது | நினைவகம் | GIL பாதிக்கப்படுமா? |
|----------|----------|--------|---------------|
| `threading` | I/O-bound | shared | Yes |
| `multiprocessing` | CPU-bound | separate | No |
| `asyncio` | I/O-bound | shared | Yes |

### The GIL
> The **Global Interpreter Lock** (GIL) allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads can still be useful for I/O — while one thread waits for network, another runs.

### முக்கிய வகுப்புகள்
- `threading.Thread(target=func)` — ஒரு தரம் (thread) உருவாக்க
- `thread.start()` — தொடங்க
- `thread.join()` — முடியும் வரை காத்திரு
- `multiprocessing.Process` — ஒரே API, தனி செயல்முறை
- `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` — உயர் நிலை கூட்டம்

> **Rule of thumb:** Use `threading` for I/O-bound (web scraping, file ops). Use `multiprocessing` for CPU-bound (number crunching, image processing).

props.code:
import threading
import time

def worker(name, delay):
    print(f'{name} starting')
    time.sleep(delay)
    print(f'{name} done')

# Create threads
t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=('Thread-1', 1))
t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=('Thread-2', 2))

t1.start()
t2.start()

t1.join()  # wait for t1
t2.join()  # wait for t2
print('All threads done')

# High-level: ThreadPoolExecutor
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    futures = [pool.submit(worker, f'W{i}', 0.1) for i in range(3)]
    for f in futures:
        f.result()

import threading

t1.start()
t2.start()
t1.join()
t2.join()

q.en: What does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) do?

en: Lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time
Stops threads from doing any I/O at the same time
Locks a shared list so threads can't append to it
Gives each thread its own separate memory
ta: ஒரே நேரத்தில் ஒரு thread மட்டுமே Python bytecode-ஐ இயக்க அனுமதிக்கிறது
threads ஒரே நேரத்தில் எந்த I/O-வும் செய்யாமல் தடுக்கிறது
threads append செய்ய முடியாதபடி பகிரப்பட்ட list-ஐ பூட்டுகிறது

q.en: You need to speed up heavy number crunching on several CPU cores. Which should you use?
q.ta: பல CPU cores-இல் கனமான எண் கணக்கீட்டை வேகப்படுத்த வேண்டும். எதைப் பயன்படுத்த வேண்டும்?

en: asyncio, since it runs code on all cores at once
multiprocessing, since separate processes avoid the GIL
ThreadPoolExecutor, since a pool bypasses the GIL
threading, since threads share memory and are faster
ta: asyncio, ஏனெனில் அது எல்லா cores-இலும் ஒரே நேரத்தில் இயங்கும்
multiprocessing, ஏனெனில் தனி processes GIL-ஐத் தவிர்க்கின்றன
ThreadPoolExecutor, ஏனெனில் pool GIL-ஐத் தாண்டிச் செல்லும்
threading, ஏனெனில் threads நினைவகத்தைப் பகிர்வதால் வேகமானவை

q.en: Spot the mistake: t = threading.Thread(target=task('a')); t.start()

en: task('a') runs at once in the main thread; use args=('a',)
Thread needs a name= argument before it can start
start() must be called before the Thread is created
Nothing is wrong; task('a') runs in the new thread
ta: task('a') main thread-இலேயே உடனே இயங்கும்; args=('a',) பயன்படுத்தவும்
Thread உருவாக்கும் முன்பே start() அழைக்கப்பட வேண்டும்
தவறு இல்லை; task('a') புதிய thread-இல் இயங்கும்

under_the_hood.summary: Threads share one process and, in standard CPython, take turns holding the GIL to run Python code, while multiprocessing starts separate interpreter processes that really run in parallel.

steps.title: A thread is an OS thread
steps.body: `threading.Thread(target=work).start()` asks the operating system for a real thread inside the same process. All threads share the same memory, so they see the same lists, dicts and globals without copying.

steps.title: The GIL lets one thread run Python at a time
steps.body: In standard CPython only the thread holding the Global Interpreter Lock may execute bytecode. A running thread is asked to release it every 5 ms (`sys.getswitchinterval()` is 0.005), so threads interleave, but CPU-heavy Python code does not get faster with more threads.

steps.title: Waiting releases the GIL
steps.body: When a thread waits on a network reply, a file read or `time.sleep`, CPython releases the GIL during the wait. Other threads run meanwhile, which is why threads speed up I/O-bound work such as downloading many pages.

steps.title: Processes sidestep the GIL
steps.body: `multiprocessing.Pool(4)` starts four separate Python processes, each with its own interpreter, memory and GIL. They can use four CPU cores at once. The cost: arguments and results are pickled and sent between processes, and starting a process takes far longer than starting a thread.

left.label: Threads
left.code:
shared memory
one GIL: Python code takes turns
good for I/O waits
cheap to start

right.label: Processes
right.code:
separate memory
one GIL each: true parallelism
good for CPU work
data pickled across

steps.title: Shared memory needs locks
steps.body: Because threads share objects, two threads doing `counter += 1` can interleave between reading and writing and lose updates. A `threading.Lock` makes the read-modify-write happen as one unit; processes avoid this by not sharing memory by default.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Rule of thumb in standard CPython: threads for waiting (I/O), processes for computing (CPU). The GIL is the reason, and switching only happens between bytecodes or during blocking calls.
